Lesson 76 ran lesson 71’s four rules over the twenty-eight moves on which all of them are defined. The 2-and-5 rule asked for 9 orders, the 3-and-10 for 2, and the 5-and-20 and 8-and-30 for 1 each.

On the same twenty-eight moves the 2-and-5 rule had a six-day stretch, moves 46 to 51, in which the position never changed and no order was sent, and it earned 0.30 in the instrument’s units. It then had five consecutive days, moves 52 to 56, of exit, entry, exit, entry, exit, and it earned 1.00 while the instrument itself rose 0.90 across the whole stretch.

A typical daily move over those twenty-eight is 0.7286. Five orders are two and a half round trips. Lesson 12 priced a round trip at a fifth of one per cent of a typical day’s movement on its index ETF and at 52 per cent of one on its micro cap.

An order reaches the market through your equipment and then through the broker, and availability along a chain multiplies. Take the broker at 99.9 per cent and a year as 8,760 hours. The book asks for 117 orders a year.

What is the chain’s availability and its downtime a year at your side of 99.0, 99.9, 99.99 and 99.999 per cent, and how many orders a year does the chain cost you at each? Then: what does a second connection do to your side, and what does a stop resting at the broker do to the hours a position spends unprotected?
Use lesson 76’s 58.5 round trips a year, lesson 67’s edge of a tenth of an R and its 589 trades and median worst drawdown of 8.82R, and the one and a half per cent a trade lesson 75 licenses.

Lesson 79 sized the capital so that the expected annual gain equals the wage, which means a cost base measured as a share of the wage is the same share of the edge. Take a cost base of a quarter of the wage on the book lesson 79 priced: 11.40 years of capital, 58.5 round trips a year, a tenth of an R, and lesson 67’s verdict at 5.8888 divided by the edge squared.

What capital does the wage plus the cost base require, what edge is left, how many trades does the verdict take, and how many years is that at 58.5 round trips a year against 480? And why does the wait move so much faster than the capital?
The pace is lesson 76’s 58.5 round trips a year.

Thirteen orders in twenty-eight days is a rate: 13 ÷ 28 × 252 = 117 orders a year, which is 58.5 round trips. The fastest rule asked for 9 of the 13, which is 9 ÷ 13 = 69.23 per cent of every order the book sent.

The verdict is one division: 589 ÷ 58.5 = 10.07 years. Forty trades a month is 480 round trips a year, so the same 589 would have taken 589 ÷ 480 = 1.23 years, and at the 240 round trips a mid-table pace gives, 2.45.

The gap between 10.07 and 1.23 is not a disagreement about patience. It is a count that was assumed against a count that was made, on the same rule family, and the assumed one is eight times the measured one. A reader carrying lesson 65’s wait in their head is carrying somebody else’s numerator.
117 orders and 58.5 round trips a year, 69.23 per cent of the workload on one rule, and a verdict 10.07 years away against 1.23 at the assumed pace.

Two divisions. 0.30 ÷ 0.7286 = 0.41 typical daily moves for the six days that asked for nothing, and 1.00 ÷ 0.7286 = 1.37 for the five days that asked for an order every session. The ratio is 1.00 ÷ 0.30 = 3.33, and it runs the opposite way from the one the shape of the fortnight suggests.

Then the bill. Two and a half round trips at a fifth of one per cent of 0.7286 is 2.5 × 0.002 × 0.7286 = 0.0036, which is 0.36 per cent of the 1.00, so the week keeps 99.6 per cent of what it made. The same two and a half round trips at 52 per cent of 0.7286 is 0.95, which is 95 per cent of the gain, so the week keeps a twentieth of it.

Identical rule, identical week, identical orders. The five days that felt like work made more than three times what the six quiet days made, so the feeling was right about which week was worth having and useless about whether it paid: that is settled entirely by which of lesson 12’s two instruments you are on.

0.41 typical daily moves against 1.37, a ratio of 3.33 the busy week’s way, and five orders costing 0.0036 on the index ETF against 0.95 on the micro cap, which keeps 99.6 per cent of the gain against a twentieth of it.

98.901, 99.800, 99.890 and 99.899 per cent, which is 96.3, 17.5, 9.6 and 8.8 hours a year and 1.29, 0.23, 0.13 and 0.12 orders missed, which flattens where the hours flatten because the last of them belong to the broker; the second connection takes your side to 99.792 per cent and the position to 27.0 unprotected hours, and the resting stop takes it to 8.8 for nothing.
The capital is one division: 1 ÷ (58.5 × 0.10 × 0.015) = 11.40 years of the wage. The verdict is another: 589 ÷ 58.5 = 10.07 years. The two horizons are the same horizon.

11.40 years of wage, a verdict 10.07 years away, 88.3 per cent drawn as wages, a share the pace cancels out of, the whole account reached at 1.70 per cent a trade, and 101.6 per cent with the drawdown added.

The capital is the wage and the cost base together: 11.40 × 1.25 = 14.25 years of wage, an extra 2.85. The edge is the same fraction gone: a quarter of the wage is a quarter of the edge, so 0.10 becomes 0.075.

The verdict is 5.8888 ÷ 0.075² = 1,047 trades, and at 58.5 round trips a year that is 17.90 years rather than 10.07. The same bill on the same account at 480 round trips a year takes 0.0030 R from each trade rather than 0.0250, leaves an edge of 0.0970, and costs 1.30 years against 1.23. Eight years at the pace you actually trade at, and a month at the pace you assumed.
14.25 years of wage, an edge of 0.075 R, 1,047 trades, and 17.90 years at the measured pace against 1.30 at the assumed one; the wait moves faster because it goes as one over the edge squared.

The last column is what ranks the work. A record twenty-two times the one you have is two years and eight months of trading the rule you already have, which is a plan. A record eighty-four times the one you have is a decade, and one a hundred and fifty times is a working life. The reachable bar is the one to start on, and it is reachable precisely because it is the one that was fixed before the first trade rather than demanded after it.
0.12, 2.67, 10.07 and 17.90 years, which is 1, 22.3, 84.1 and 149.6 times the record; the fixed horizon at 22.3 times is the reachable one; and every item on the list is a subtraction.

Whether you can put a count where an assumption was. Handed a grid, you count the orders it actually asked for and turn that into a pace; handed a quiet stretch and a busy one, you price both and find that the one which felt like work made three times the other and then lost almost all of it to the wrong instrument; handed a chain, you multiply it and stop buying at the link you do not own; handed a rate, you ask what share of a loss comes back rather than what the rate is; handed a wage, you divide it by the edge, the pace and the risk per trade and read the years off; handed a fixed cost, you divide it among the trades there actually are; and handed a record, you set it against every bar the course wrote and work on the smallest gap that is not already closed.

Module 11 is where the candidates come from, and it starts where this book is weakest. This one carries 1.04 independent bets on a single instrument, and lesson 82 asks what a second instrument does to it: two rules on each of two instruments is four positions, and at a cross-correlation of zero that is 2.13 bets rather than four.
